The city had a department for everything, including things it preferred not to discuss.

There was a Department of Bridges, a Department of Sanitation, and a Department of Trees Whose Roots Had Become Everybody’s Problem. There was an office that issued permits for music after ten at night. There was another that collected the permits and denied having issued them.

In the basement of the municipal building, behind a door marked STORAGE, was the Department of Unfinished Things.

Mara found it on a Tuesday while looking for a bathroom.

Inside, a man in a cardigan sat beneath a clock with no minute hand. Behind him stood rows of shelves containing objects that seemed ordinary until she looked closely: a scarf ending in a knitting needle, a chessboard midgame, a letter with only “Dear” written at the top.

“Name?” the man asked.

“I’m just looking for—”

“Most people are.”

He opened a ledger.

“Mara Vale,” she said, although she couldn’t have explained why.

The man ran one finger down a page. “You have quite a collection.”

“I’m sorry?”

He stood, fetched a cardboard box from a shelf, and placed it on the counter. Her name was written on the lid in her own handwriting.

Inside was the blue notebook in which she had once intended to write a novel. Underneath lay a plane ticket to Lisbon, a packet of tomato seeds, and a photograph of her younger brother.

“That’s mine,” she said.

“Yes.”

“How did you get it?”

“Things arrive.”

The photograph had been taken beside a river. Her brother was seventeen, all elbows and certainty, squinting into the sun. Mara remembered the argument afterward. He had called her afraid of everything. She had told him fear was a reasonable response to knowing him.

That had been twelve years ago.

He was alive. That was somehow worse for the purposes of the box.

“I don’t understand.”

“Would you like the official explanation?”

“Would that help?”

“Rarely.”

He took the lid and set it beneath the box.

“We store what people leave unfinished. Not everything, obviously. Nobody has shelf space for every abandoned sandwich. Only the things that keep taking up room after they’re gone.”

Mara touched the notebook. She had last seen it in an apartment she no longer remembered fondly.

“Can I take them?”

“One at a time.”

“Why?”

“We tried allowing more. People became ambitious. It caused a backlog.”

She looked again at the photograph.

The man said nothing.

“What happens if I leave them here?”

“Nothing.”

“Forever?”

“We don’t use that word in municipal government.”

Mara almost laughed.

She chose the tomato seeds.

The clerk nodded without approval or disappointment. He stamped a form and handed her the packet.

Outside, rain had darkened the pavement. She stood under the municipal building’s stone awning and read the instructions.

Sow indoors six to eight weeks before the last frost.

It was September.

For the first time all afternoon, this struck her as genuinely inconvenient.

***

She returned the next Tuesday.

“I planted them,” she said.

The clerk looked up. “Good morning.”

“In pots. On the windowsill. I know it’s the wrong season.”

“Plants don’t read.”

“They’re going to die.”

“Possibly.”

She waited for something wiser.

He continued sharpening a pencil.

“I’d like the notebook.”

He brought down the box.

At home, Mara opened it to the first page. There was a title, crossed out three times. Then a sentence:

*When the sea disappeared, everybody blamed the mayor.*

She remembered writing it. She remembered being delighted.

On the next page were seventeen reasons the idea wouldn’t work.

She tore out that page.

Then she regretted tearing it out and put it back between the covers.

For an hour she wrote badly. The mayor acquired a wife, then lost her because Mara couldn’t decide what she wanted. A fisherman discovered his boat balanced on the roof of the aquarium. Someone stole all the salt from the supermarkets.

At midnight, she stopped.

The sea was still missing. Nobody had explained anything.

She slept better than she had in months.

***

On her third visit, the clerk wasn’t there.

A woman sat at the counter eating an orange.

“Where’s the man?”

“Dentist.”

Mara felt foolishly relieved.

“I’d like something from my box.”

The woman retrieved it, then turned back to peeling the orange.

The plane ticket was expired. The notebook was at home. The seeds had become six pale stems bending toward the window.

Only the photograph remained.

Mara picked it up.

“Do you have a phone?” she asked.

The woman pointed to one beside the ledger.

Her brother’s number had survived three phones and several declarations that she intended to delete it.

He answered on the fourth ring.

“Mara?”

She watched the woman place a curl of orange peel on a napkin.

“I found a picture of you,” she said.

“All right.”

“By the river.”

He was quiet.

“You looked ridiculous,” she said.

“You took it.”

“I know.”

Neither of them apologized. Not then.

He told her he had moved. She told him about the tomatoes.

“It’s September,” he said.

“I’m aware.”

He laughed, and she recognized it before she recognized how much she had missed it.

***

In December, the plants produced one tomato.

It was small, crooked, and mostly green. Mara put it on the kitchen table and called her brother to report the harvest.

He suggested frying it.

She said that seemed disrespectful.

“Of course,” he said. “Better to let it rot.”

She found a pan.

While the oil heated, she opened her notebook. The sea had returned during the night, filling the streets with cold water. She had no idea what happened next.
